raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old woman, 22 weeks pregnant, was referred to our unit by our obstetric colleagues with a 1-day history of severe macroscopic haematuria. Further medical history noted that she had been diagnosed with HIV 2 months prior with a CD4+ count of 38 cells/mm3 and an HIV viral load of 1259 copies/ml at diagnosis. She had been initiated on antiretroviral therapy and has been compliant with treatment since. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date. On initial examination, she was acutely ill, pale, tachycardic and tachypnoeic with a blood pressure of 112/71 mmHg. Her haemoglobin level was 6.2 g/dl. The rest of her examination, including a pelvic exam, was unremarkable. The bedside kidney-ureter-bladder (KUB) ultrasound was unremarkable, apart from a diffusely thickened bladder wall. A live, intrauterine singleton pregnancy with a gestation of 22 weeks was confirmed by transabdominal ultrasound.
She was admitted for intravenous fluid, and blood product resuscitation and continuous bladder irrigation were initiated.
A subsequent rigid cystoscopy demonstrated multiple areas of oedematous and erythematous bladder urothelium with areas of normal mucosa in between (Figure 1). Multiple bladder biopsies were performed using a cold cup biopsy forceps, and urine was sent for cytological analysis and microscopy and culture.
Histopathological analysis of the bladder biopsy demonstrated multiple urothelial mucosal fragments infiltrated by a prominent mixed inflammatory population comprising neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils and involving most of the fragments (Figure 2). In addition, multiple scattered cells throughout the fragments exhibited a viral cytopathy by way of enlarged nuclei with ill-defined basophilic to amphophilic intranuclear inclusions and paler amphophilic but similar large intracytoplasmic inclusions (Figure 2). These findings were morphologically consistent with a CMV infection and associated subacute cystitis, which was subsequently confirmed with positive CMV immunohistochemical stains (Figure 2). Her serum CMV viral load count was 113,383 IU/ml.
After a multidisciplinary team discussion with the patient regarding the benefits and risks of treatment, a combined decision was made to initiate antiviral therapy. She was commenced on 12 hourly intravenous Ganciclovir at a dose of 5 mg/kg for 14 days. It was decided not to continue her on an oral maintenance therapy in order to limit foetal exposure to the drug. Her haematuria promptly resolved after the initiation of antiviral therapy, and she was discharged after completing her course of antiviral treatment. Her pregnancy continued uncomplicated, and she delivered a healthy male infant at 38 weeks of gestation. The newborn was asymptomatic at birth, and viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR), audiology assessment, cranial ultrasound and neurodevelopmental assessment were reassuring. Six months post-partum, both the mother and infant are well with no signs or symptoms of active CMV disease or any signs of congenital CMV infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks of gestation presented with a 1-day history of severe macroscopic hematuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, previously uncomplicated at 22 weeks of gestation, was referred by obstetric colleagues after developing acute, severe macroscopic hematuria for 1 day.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV 2 months prior to presentation (baseline CD4+ count 38 cells/mm3 and HIV viral load 1,259 copies/mL at diagnosis), compliant on antiretroviral therapy (ART) since diagnosis. Current singleton intrauterine pregnancy at 22 weeks of gestation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe macroscopic hematuria. Compliant with home antiretroviral therapy.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill, pale, tachycardic, and tachypneic with blood pressure 112/71 mmHg. Rest of physical examination, including pelvic examination, was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL. Bedside kidney-ureter-bladder (KUB) ultrasound was unremarkable except for a diffusely thickened bladder wall; transabdominal ultrasound confirmed a live intrauterine singleton pregnancy at 22 weeks of gestation. Urine sent for cytology, microscopy, and culture.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ count 38 cells/mm3 (HIV viral load 1,259 copies/mL at diagnosis 2 months prior). Rigid cystoscopy demonstrated multiple areas of edematous and erythematous bladder urothelium interspersed with normal mucosa. Cold-cup bladder mucosal biopsies showed urothelial fragments infiltrated by a mixed inflammatory population (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils) and scattered cells with viral cytopathy featuring enlarged nuclei with ill-defined basophilic-to-amphophilic intranuclear inclusions and paler amphophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cytomegalovirus (CMV)-associated subacute hemorrhagic cystitis in pregnancy confirmed by characteristic intranuclear and intracytoplasmic viral inclusions on bladder biopsy, positive CMV immunohistochemical (IHC) staining, and elevated serum CMV viral load of 113,383 IU/mL. Initial management included IV fluid and blood product resuscitation and continuous bladder irrigation. Treated with intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg every 12 hours for 14 days (oral maintenance therapy withheld to limit fetal exposure). Macroscopic hematuria promptly resolved, and she delivered a healthy, asymptomatic male infant at 38 weeks of gestation (neonatal CMV PCR, audiology, cranial ultrasound, and neurodevelopmental assessments were normal). At 6 months postpartum, both mother and infant remained well without active or congenital CMV disease.
